questions.q: ___ am going to the cinema tonight.
questions.why: Use the subject pronoun 'I' before the verb as the doer of the action.

questions.q: Can you help ___ with this box?
questions.why: Use the object pronoun 'me' after a verb as the receiver of the action.

questions.q: ___ is a doctor at the local hospital.
questions.why: Use the subject pronoun 'He' before the verb as the subject.

questions.q: I saw ___ at the party last night.
questions.why: Use the object pronoun 'him' after the verb 'saw'.

questions.q: This is ___ book; please don't take it.
questions.why: 'My' is a possessive adjective and must come before a noun like 'book'.

questions.q: That book is ___, not yours.
questions.why: 'Mine' is a possessive pronoun that stands alone without a noun after it.

questions.q: Is this ___ coat or hers?
questions.why: 'Your' is a possessive adjective and comes before the noun 'coat'.

questions.q: The red umbrella is ___.
questions.why: 'Yours' is a possessive pronoun used alone, with no noun following.

questions.q: I cut ___ while chopping vegetables.
questions.why: Use the reflexive 'myself' when the subject and object are the same person.

questions.q: The children dressed ___ for school.
questions.why: The correct reflexive for 'they' is 'themselves'; 'theirselves' is not standard.

questions.q: He hurt ___ playing football.
questions.why: Use 'himself' because the subject 'he' acts on the same person.

questions.q: Tom and Jerry always help ___.
questions.why: Use 'each other' when two people do the same thing to one another.

questions.q: The woman ___ lives next door is a nurse.
questions.why: Use 'who' as a relative pronoun for people who are the subject.

questions.q: That's the car ___ I want to buy.
questions.why: Use 'which' as a relative pronoun for things, not people.

questions.q: ___ and I went to the market together.
questions.why: In the subject 'He and I', use the subject pronoun 'He'.

questions.q: She gave the tickets to John and ___.
questions.why: After the preposition 'to', use the object pronoun 'me'.

questions.q: We enjoyed ___ at the beach.
questions.why: The reflexive for 'we' is 'ourselves' when the action returns to the subject.

questions.q: Whose phone is this? It's ___.
questions.why: 'Hers' is a possessive pronoun used alone, without a following noun.

questions.q: The students looked at ___ in the mirror.
questions.why: Each student looked at his or her own reflection, so use the reflexive 'themselves'.

questions.q: Do you know the man ___ car is parked outside?
questions.why: 'Whose' is the relative pronoun showing possession.

questions.q: It was ___ who broke the window, not us.
questions.why: After 'It was', formal English uses the subject pronoun 'they'.

questions.q: Please pass ___ the salt.
questions.why: 'Me' is the object pronoun receiving the action of passing.

questions.q: Type the answer: '___ (subject pronoun for yourself) and Sarah are good friends.'
questions.why: Use the subject pronoun 'I' as part of the subject 'I and Sarah'.

questions.q: Type the answer: 'She made the cake ___ (reflexive for she), with no help.'
questions.why: Use 'herself' when the subject does the action alone or to herself.

questions.q: Type the answer: 'This pen isn't mine; it's ___ (belonging to you, used alone).'
questions.why: 'Yours' is a possessive pronoun used without a noun after it.

questions.q: Type the answer: 'The two brothers wrote letters to ___ ___ for years.' (two-word phrase meaning one another)
questions.why: Use 'each other' for an action two people do to one another.

questions.q: Type the answer: 'I bought ___ (possessive adjective for me) ticket online.'
questions.why: 'My' is a possessive adjective and comes before the noun 'ticket'.

questions.q: Type the answer: 'Give the book to ___ (object pronoun for him).'
questions.why: After the preposition 'to', use the object pronoun 'him'.

questions.q: Type the answer: 'The dog hurt ___ (reflexive) when it jumped the fence.'
questions.why: Use 'itself' as the reflexive pronoun for an animal or thing.

questions.q: Type the answer: 'The teacher ___ (relative pronoun for a person) taught us has retired.'
questions.why: Use 'who' as the relative pronoun referring to a person who is the subject.
